title: Autonomy: The Quest to Build the Driverless Car—and How It Will Reshape Our World
author: Lawrence D. Burns; Christopher Shulgan
note: Selected for technology-industry review praise and Goodreads 4.13/952. IEEE Spectrum's Mark Harris praises the engineering narrative but identifies Waymo loyalty and omitted security, congestion and social risks. Transportation writer Edward Niedermeyer also distinguishes the valuable development history from optimistic forecasts. This is a narrative of engineering and organizational change, not technical training. Its historical value does not depend primarily on forecasts coming true, so no V4 veto is established; forecasts are not treated as current facts. Technical production dominates over politics or environmental advocacy. US development has global technological influence, so thematic deductions are zero.
notes: Insider access supports the development history; company ties and omitted risks weaken the broader forecasts.
Links sensors, software, automotive engineering, research competitions, business models and regulation.
Useful contrasts between established production organizations and experimental development teams.
Explains development obstacles and organizational choices, though safety validation receives less depth.
D=7.5, moderate confidence from Harris, Niedermeyer, contents and reader reports. DARPA trials and later deployment add different constraints; visionary passages provide less established learning.
Engineering history will last; adoption and economic forecasts are less durable.
Direct fit to computing, engineering, transport and technological change.
Author's automotive R&D experience offers access, with a disclosed commercial perspective.
Clear narrative progression makes a technically complex development readable.
Accessible prose sometimes becomes promotional.

title: Ghost on the Throne: The Death of Alexander the Great and the War for Crown and Empire
author: James Romm
note: Selected: classicist Daniel Mendelsohn's praise is reproduced by the University of Michigan classics reading site; Choice named it an Outstanding Academic Title; Goodreads 4.29/3,401 corroborates reader reception. Historical explanation, not fiction, doctrine or a technical curriculum. Succession failure, unstable military loyalty and coordination around a dead ruler offer transferable mechanisms, so V3 does not apply. Political personalities and war dominate, warranting both thematic deductions; the ancient period incurs capped H13=-12. The endpoint approximates the extinction of Alexander's immediate dynasty, not a claim that the entire successor era ended then.
notes: Ancient sources and explicit notes support the reconstruction; motives and some chronology remain uncertain.
Connects dynastic legitimacy, armies, geography and fragmented imperial administration.
Succession and coordination failures generalize beyond individual rulers.
Explains incentives behind shifting alliances and unstable commitments.

D=8, moderate confidence from specialist praise, professional reviews, contents and inspected source notes. Distinct succession crises add institutional detail; many names burden retention without proving padding.
Institutional failure and succession remain durable subjects.
Some strategic and institutional relevance, little technology or production.
Classics scholar with academic recognition and specialist praise.
Clear organization sustains a complicated ensemble narrative.
Controlled prose with explicit source qualifications.

title: The Eagle and the Hart: The Tragedy of Richard II and Henry IV
author: Helen Castor
note: Selected: historian Kathryn Hughes praises the book; Women's Prize judge Leah Broad also commends its detailed political study. Goodreads 4.40/1,761 supports strong reader reception. The account explains legitimacy, fiscal constraints and limits to personal rule rather than only listing royal events, so it passes V3. It is neither doctrinal advocacy nor partisan recruitment. English royal politics is a weak topic fit, with both thematic deductions and capped historical deduction. High praise does not imply a high personalized score.
notes: Document-based scholarship supports the history; psychological interpretations remain less certain than recorded actions.
Connects royal authority, parliamentary finance, war and elite allegiance.
Shows how legitimate title and practical ability can diverge, and how fiscal dependence constrains rulers.
Explains failures of authority, but gives considerable weight to personality.

D=7.5, moderate confidence from professional reviews, author research account and reader response. Contrasting reigns add institutional comparisons; extensive court detail has lower yield for this collection. No full-text density audit.
The constraints on personal rule remain durable.
Institutional power fits partly, but engineering and production are largely absent.
Established medieval historian working directly with parliamentary and other records.
Chronological dual biography makes complex political changes readable.
Precise and vivid narrative writing.
